hotel_name: Four Seasons Resort Sharm El Sheikh
highlights: Dramatic Red Sea oasis cascading from Sinai desert cliffs to coral-rich reef
description:
Four Seasons Resort Sharm El Sheikh occupies a terraced Red Sea estate at Shark Bay, where Sinai desert slopes descend toward clear water and coral reefs. The resort feels deliberately expansive: gardens of more than 3,000 palms, shaded paths and funiculars link hilltop arrivals with a one-kilometre private beachfront, while the wider setting places Ras Mohammed National Park, Mount Sinai and Saint Catherine's Monastery within reach for longer excursions.

The resort has 289 accommodations, including rooms, chalets, villas and 56 suites, with many oriented to sea, garden or private-pool views. Its architecture draws on Arabian and Egyptian references without losing resort ease: pale stone, arches, terraces and lush landscaping frame the meeting of desert, reef and sky. The scale allows for both quiet corners and more residential villa-style spaces, with terraced clusters and shaded garden paths helping the resort feel private despite its breadth.

Dining is broad enough to make the property feel like a complete Red Sea village. Bullona brings Mediterranean seafood, Yatai focuses on Japanese and Pan-Asian cooking, Zitouni serves Lebanese flavours, Il Frantoio is Italian, Arabesque explores regional Middle Eastern dishes, and Reef Grill stays close to the beach with grilled seafood and meats. Lounges and poolside venues add sunset, Latin and relaxed daytime moods.

Leisure is rooted in the water. The on-site dive centre gives direct access to Sharm El Sheikh's celebrated reefs and nearby wreck sites, while snorkelling, yacht charters and watersports extend the marine focus. Four outdoor pools, tennis courts, a spa with 13 treatment rooms, a fitness centre, a kids' club and desert safaris round out a resort shaped equally by reef, sand and Sinai horizons.

highlights: Cloud-skimming IFC tower retreat with Pearl River views and Michelin-starred Cantonese dining
description:
Four Seasons Hotel Guangzhou rises through the upper third of the 103-storey Guangzhou International Finance Center in Zhujiang New Town, the city's contemporary business and cultural district. The address looks across the Pearl River toward Canton Tower and sits close to the Zaha Hadid-designed Guangzhou Opera House, Guangdong Museum and the malls, offices and promenades of the new city centre.

The hotel has 344 rooms and suites, all set high above the skyline. Its most theatrical interior gesture is a 34-floor atrium climbing from the 70th-floor lobby, a vertical space that makes the hotel feel suspended within the tower rather than simply placed inside it. Wilkinson Eyre designed the building, while interiors by HBA, AB Concept and Steve Leung balance international polish with Chinese details, contemporary art and refreshed rooms that draw on Lingnan heritage.

Dining is a major strength. Yu Yue Heen, the hotel's Cantonese restaurant, holds one Michelin star in the 2025 Guangzhou guide and has been recognised for refined local cooking, seasonal seafood and precise dim sum. Catch occupies a dramatic high-floor setting for contemporary French dining, Kumoi brings Japanese cuisine, Caffe Mondo is the all-day Italian address, and Tian Bar and The Atrium turn the tower's height into evening theatre.

Hua Spa sits on the 69th floor, spreading across 1,866 square metres with eight treatment rooms, crystal steam, laconium, ice and hydrotherapy facilities. A 22-metre indoor lap pool, fitness centre and Executive Club on the 99th floor add to the sense of a complete sky-level urban retreat, well placed for both commerce and Guangzhou's cultural landmarks.

hotel_name: Four Seasons Resort Bali at Sayan
highlights: Suspended above the Ayung Valley, a spiritual jungle retreat shaped by Balinese ritual
description:
Four Seasons Resort Bali at Sayan is set in the Ayung River valley, a few kilometres from central Ubud and surrounded by forest, rice terraces and village life. Arrival is part of the architecture: a suspension bridge leads toward the circular rooftop lotus pond and bowl-like reception pavilion, before the resort drops into the valley in a sequence of paths, gardens and river-facing terraces.

The resort has 60 accommodations, made up of 18 suites and 42 villas. Designed by John Heah with interiors shaped by Design Studio SPIN, it translates Balinese landscape and ritual into a highly sculptural resort language. Suites sit within the main building, while villas bring private pools and outdoor living spaces closer to the forest and river. Despite its design pedigree, the mood remains intimate, with temple visits, artisan villages, Ubud's galleries and the surrounding highlands forming the broader cultural setting.

Dining keeps close to place. Ayung Terrace serves modern Indonesian cooking above the valley, Riverside moves toward Mediterranean flavours by the water, and Sokasi presents Balinese tasting menus, cooking classes and a more ceremonial village-kitchen atmosphere. Jati Bar, open to the forest, brings the resort's social life into a breezy, elevated lounge.

Sacred River Spa is a defining feature, redesigned across 4,970 square metres with seven spa villas, two yoga pavilions and treatments shaped by Balinese healing traditions. Wellness extends to meditation, yoga, sound work and the resort's signature Sacred Nap. River rafting, biking, farming experiences, cooking classes, art encounters and the Pici Pici kids' club make the property feel connected to both Ubud's creative culture and the rhythms of the Ayung.

highlights: Mile-long Tanjung Rhu beachfront framed by limestone cliffs and mangrove wilderness
description:
Four Seasons Resort Langkawi stretches along Tanjung Rhu on the island's quieter northern coast, where pale sand, the Andaman Sea and limestone cliffs meet the protected landscapes of the Langkawi UNESCO Global Geopark. Kilim Karst Geoforest Park lies close by, giving the resort an immediate link to mangrove channels, ancient sea stacks, hornbills and coastal ecology rather than only beach leisure.

The resort has 92 accommodations, divided between 68 pavilions and 24 villas. Its design blends traditional Malay kampung references with Moorish and broader Asian influences, using low-slung architecture, generous pavilions and carefully framed outdoor spaces to keep the landscape close. Carved details, indoor-outdoor living and garden pathways create a setting that feels spacious and rooted in the tropics, with pavilions close to landscaped gardens and villas oriented toward beach, sea or family privacy.

Restaurants give the resort a strong regional character. Ikan-Ikan focuses on Malaysian cooking under open-air roofs, HAVA brings northwestern Indian flavours, Serai is the international breakfast and all-day venue, and Kelapa Grill moves from daytime ease to local seafood and Josper-grilled meats by night. Rhu Bar adds the sunset address, with the beach and islands in view.

The Geo Spa is set amid limestone cliffs and reflecting ponds, with six treatment rooms and rituals inspired by the island's geology. Two pools, a fitness centre, tennis, watersports, bicycles, jogging paths and Kids for All Seasons support resort days, while guided nature walks, kayaking and naturalist-led mangrove safaris reveal the older, wilder Langkawi beyond the sand.

highlights: Gwanghwamun sophistication with palace views, Korean artistry and Michelin-starred Cantonese dining
description:
Four Seasons Hotel Seoul stands on Saemunan-ro in Gwanghwamun, placing it in the historic and civic centre of the capital. Gyeongbokgung Palace, Cheonggyecheon Stream, Seoul Plaza, government buildings, museums and the shopping districts of Myeongdong and Insadong are all part of the surrounding urban fabric, while mountain and palace views give many rooms a strong sense of place.

The hotel has 317 accommodations, including 285 rooms and 32 suites. Its design is contemporary but threaded with Korean references: refined stone and timber, geometric patterning and more than 160 works of contemporary art create a polished urban atmosphere rather than a heritage pastiche. Large windows bring the city into the rooms, while the location makes the hotel a natural base for palace walks, gallery visits, business meetings and evening cocktails in one of Seoul's most expressive districts.

Dining is extensive and sophisticated. Yu Yuan, the 11th-floor Cantonese restaurant led by Chef To Kwok Wai, holds one Michelin star in the 2026 South Korea guide. Akira Back adds modern Japanese-Korean cooking, Boccalino is the Italian restaurant, The Market Kitchen serves international cuisine, and Maru is the social Korean lounge. Charles H., H.Bar, OUL and Confections give the hotel a notably strong bar and patisserie collection.

Wellness occupies a generous city-hotel footprint. The spa has seven treatment rooms, a nail bar, barbershop and Korean sauna facilities, while a 765-square-metre fitness club, indoor pool, children's plunge pool and golf simulation area support daily routines. An Executive Club, event spaces, the Garden Terrace and an on-site Nicolai Bergmann floral studio reinforce the property's role as both luxury hotel and polished Seoul social address.
